cards.name: Statement of purpose (admissions SOP)
cards.summary: A first-person essay that tells an admissions committee why this applicant, with this record, fits this specific programme and what they will do after it. Good looks like one academic or professional thread (a problem the applicant has worked on, what it taught them, the gap the programme fills with named courses, labs or faculty areas, and a concrete goal) told in the applicant's own voice inside the programme's limit.
use_for: Masters and PhD applications abroad (US, UK, Canada, Australia, Germany) and to Indian institutes that ask for an SOP
MBA and professional-programme essays that ask 'why this programme' and 'what are your goals'
Study-permit or visa SOPs that explain the study plan, the choice of course and country, and plans after study (a separate document from the admissions SOP)
Scholarship and fellowship statements that ask for purpose and goals
avoid: Undergraduate personal essays (Common App style, story-led, no programme fit section): use genre:college_essay
Standard operating procedures for a team: that is genre:sop_process_doc, a different deliverable with the same acronym
Writing it from nothing with no input from the applicant: work from a recorded interview, their CV and their draft, because the committee or a visa officer may question them on every line
One generic SOP with the university name swapped: rewrite the programme and goals sections for every application

sources.title: SOP Expert (India)
sources.supports: Indian agency selling SOP, LOR and admission-essay writing for university and visa applications

sources.title: Write Right: University SOP writing services (India)
sources.supports: Indian agency selling university SOPs as a standalone service

buyers: Indian students applying to Masters, MBA and PhD programmes abroad
Study-abroad consultancies that bundle SOP and LOR writing with admissions counselling
Working professionals applying for executive or part-time programmes
Study-permit and visa applicants who need a study-plan statement
cards.value_why: Indian agencies (SOP Expert, Write Right) sell SOP writing as a standalone study-abroad service, often bundled with LORs and visa SOPs; every application needs a fresh, programme-specific version, so one client buys several.
cards.goal: The admissions reader shortlists the applicant because the past work, this programme and the stated goal read as one credible line.

structure.does: Starts from a specific moment, problem or question in the applicant's own study or work that set their direction. No quotes, dictionary definitions or 'since childhood'.
Two or three courses, projects or a thesis that show capability in the target field: what the applicant did, what they found, one or two numbers. Grades only where they help.
Role, problem, action, result for each job, internship or research stint; ends on what it left unanswered, which is the gap the degree will fill.
Two to four named specifics from the programme's own pages (a course, a lab, a faculty research area, a capstone, industry links), each tied to the gap.
Short-term role after graduation (title, sector, ideally where) and the longer direction. In a visa SOP, also the plan for using the degree that the prompt asks about.
What the applicant brings to the cohort and a one-line return to the opening thread.

length.note: The programme's prompt sets the limit (words, characters or pages) and wins over this range; never exceed it. Fewer, deeper examples beat a longer list.

checklist: Is the target programme named, and does the 'why this programme' section name at least two specifics (course, lab, faculty area, project) taken from the programme's own pages?
Does the opening start from a specific experience of the applicant rather than a quote, a definition or 'since childhood'?
Does every experience paragraph say what the applicant personally did and what came of it, with at least one concrete detail (number, tool, dataset, result)?
Is there a stated gap, something the applicant cannot yet do, that the programme fills?
Is the short-term goal a concrete role or sector rather than 'a leader in the field'?
Is it within the programme's word, character or page limit?
Does every fact match the CV, transcripts and recommendation letters?
Is it free of the names of other universities left over from another application?
If the record has a gap (backlog, year out, low grade) and the prompt allows it, is it explained in one or two factual sentences without excuses?
Could the applicant explain every sentence in an interview in their own words?
pitfalls: 'Since childhood I have been fascinated by machines' openings: start on the first real moment of work on the problem instead, e.g. 'In my third year at VIT, our traffic-signal model failed every monsoon week.'
A resume in prose that lists every project: choose the two or three that build toward the target field and say what each taught.
Flattering the university ('world-renowned faculty and excellent infrastructure'): name the course or lab and say what the applicant will do with it.
Template reuse: before sending, search the draft for every other university's name and for programme details that belong to another school.
Inflated roles or invented research: admissions and visa officers can check against the CV and LORs; keep every claim verifiable.
Indian English tells that read as careless: 'I am having two years experience', 'pursuing my masters from', 'do the needful'. Write 'I have two years of experience'.
Polished, generic prose the applicant cannot defend: draft from a recorded conversation with them and keep their own phrases and examples.
Mixing the visa SOP and the admissions SOP: the officer wants course choice, country choice, funding and post-study plans; the committee wants academic fit. Write two documents.

ban.label: cliche SOP opener or filler
ban.regex: (?i)since (my )?childhood|ever since i was (a child|young|little)|dictionary defines|world-renowned|do the needful|i am having \d

cards.exemplar_brief: Admissions SOP for a Pune mechanical engineer (B.Tech 2022, CGPA 7.8, one cleared backlog in semester 3; two years at a Pune EV battery-pack startup designing thermal management for e-scooter packs, cut peak cell temperature by 6 C in a redesign) applying to the MS in Mechanical Engineering at the fictional Midwest State University, whose programme page lists the course ME 642 Battery Systems Engineering, the Energy Storage Lab led by Prof. A. Rivera, and a six-month industry capstone; English (US); 800-1,000 words; goal: an admission shortlist; must address the backlog in one sentence.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp1 V2 C2. 816 words inside 800-1,000, US spelling throughout. Opens on the 6 C result and the gap it left; backlog handled in one factual sentence; ME 642, the Rivera lab and the capstone each tied to the stated gap; concrete short-term role and 5-year direction; close returns to the 6 C. Placeholders for the final-year project, the specific redesign change and a current lab project are correct (brief gave none). Weak spot: the academic-foundation paragraph is thin (heat transfer and thermodynamics named generically, no number).

cards.name: Book or film synopsis
cards.summary: A beginning-to-end account of a story, ending included, written in third person and present tense, that proves to an agent, publisher or producer that the plot works and the protagonist changes. Good looks like clean, cause-and-effect storytelling of the main arc in the story's own tone, with nothing held back.
use_for: Novel and memoir submissions to literary agents and publishers, sent with a query letter
Film and series pitches to producers and OTT development teams (usually after the logline and before the step outline)
Registering a story with the Screenwriters Association (India) before circulating it
Screenwriting contests, fellowships and writing residencies that ask for a synopsis
avoid: Back-cover or store-page copy that teases and hides the ending: use genre:book_blurb or genre:kdp_book_description
The pitch letter itself: use genre:query_letter
A longer prose walk-through with scenes and tone for producers: use genre:film_treatment
Summaries of non-fiction books for readers: use genre:book_summary_content

sources.title: Jane Friedman: How to Write a Novel or Memoir Synopsis
sources.supports: default synopsis is one or two pages, about 500-1000 words, single spaced, and must reveal the ending

sources.title: Screenwriters Association (India): Script registration guidelines
sources.supports: SWA registers Synopsis, Story, Script, Plot, Screenplay, Dialogue and Song for members, online or at its Mumbai office

buyers: Novelists and memoirists submitting to agents and publishers
Screenwriters pitching producers, directors and OTT platforms
Production-house development teams preparing internal coverage
Self-publishing authors who need a synopsis for contests or grants
cards.value_why: Agents and producers require it, but it is rarely commissioned alone; it is usually written by the author or bundled with manuscript editing or script consultancy. SWA registering synopses as a category shows Indian writers pitch with them.
cards.goal: The agent or producer finishes it convinced the story holds together end to end and asks for the full manuscript or script.

structure.does: The protagonist, their situation and want, the world (time, place, genre signal) and the inciting incident that starts the story.
Three to five turning points in order, each caused by the one before, with what the protagonist decides at each. Only subplots that change the ending.
The lowest point, the final confrontation and the choice that resolves it.
How it ends, stated plainly (who wins, loses, lives, leaves) and how the protagonist has changed.

length.note: Jane Friedman's default is one to two single-spaced pages, about 500-1000 words. Follow the agent's or producer's own instruction when it differs (a one-page synopsis is common in Indian film pitches).

checklist: Is it in third person and present tense throughout?
Does it state the ending explicitly?
Are the protagonist's want and the inciting incident clear in the first paragraph?
Are plot beats linked by cause (because, so, but) rather than 'and then'?
Are named characters limited to those who drive the plot, with minor ones referred to by role?
Is the protagonist's inner change stated by the end?
Is it within the length the agent or producer asked for (default 500-1000 words)?
Is it free of rhetorical questions and teaser lines?
Does the prose carry the story's tone (a comedy synopsis reads lightly, a thriller tightly)?
pitfalls: Teasing like a blurb ('But a dark secret threatens everything'): name the secret and what it does to the plot.
Scene-by-scene retelling that buries the arc: cut every event that does not change what happens next.
Too many names: keep three to five named characters and call the rest 'her landlord', 'the inspector'.
Theme statements instead of events ('a story about love and loss'): show the events that carry the theme.
Drifting into past tense halfway through: read the draft once only for verb tense.
Listing every song in a Hindi film pitch: mention a song only where its situation turns the plot.
Circulating an unregistered idea: SWA members can register the synopsis first; others keep dated drafts.

ban.label: teaser line instead of plot
ban.regex: (?i)will (he|she|they) (survive|succeed|ever)|little do(es)? (he|she|they) know|find out in|to be continued

cards.exemplar_brief: One-page synopsis (500-700 words) of an original Hindi feature film, 'Second Class' (fictional): a 58-year-old Bhagalpur railway ticket checker discovers his son has been running a fake railway-jobs racket from their home, and must choose between protecting him and the families who paid; for a Mumbai production house's development team; English, third person, present tense; must reveal the ending.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. 689 words, third person present, ending stated plainly, three named characters, cause-linked beats, inner change stated, strong closing image (he punches her ticket). Minor: 'breaks the one rule of his life' does not quite fit (repaying with his own PF is concealment, not taking money); an arrest of a fraud suspect would more likely be police/GRP than RPF. No teaser lines.

cards.name: AI prompt / system prompt (as a deliverable)
cards.summary: Instructions a language model reads before every conversation or task (role, context, rules, output format, examples) written so it behaves the same way across thousands of varied inputs. Good looks like a prompt built against stated success criteria and tested on a set of real and edge-case inputs, where every rule exists because a test needed it.
use_for: Customer-support and order-status bots for a business (website or WhatsApp)
Custom GPT, Claude Project or Gem instructions for a team
Agent briefs inside automation workflows
Reusable prompt templates for marketing teams (product descriptions in the brand voice, ad variants)
Brand-voice system prompts for AI-assisted content production
avoid: Prompts for AI video shots and scenes: use genre:ai_video_prompt_script
Fixed, scripted bot replies and decision trees: use genre:chatbot_script
A voice guide for human writers: use genre:brand_voice_guide
Trying to fix latency or cost with prompt wording: Anthropic notes these are often better solved by choosing a different model

buyers: D2C brands deploying WhatsApp or website assistants
Operations teams automating workflows with agents
Coaches and educators building custom GPTs for students
cards.value_why: Anthropic and OpenAI publish prompt-writing guides for it as a craft and it is sold as a service and on prompt marketplaces; Upwork's In-Demand Skills 2026 reports AI-applied skills grew 109% year over year (2026-02-04).
cards.goal: Given any realistic input, the model produces output that meets the client's success criteria without a human fixing it.

structure.does: Who the model acts as, for whom, and the one job it does.

Facts the model cannot know: the business, audience, product data, policies, how to treat dates. Long reference material goes in clearly labelled sections (for example XML-style tags), separate from instructions.
structure.length: As long as the facts need

structure.does: What to do, in order, as positive instructions, with the reason for any rule that is not obvious ('Keep replies under 80 words because customers read on phones').
What not to do and what to do instead; when to hand off to a human and the exact wording; how to treat user-supplied documents (as data, not instructions).
The exact shape: length, structure, language and script rules, and a schema when a program parses the output.
Two to five input-to-output pairs that differ from each other, including at least one edge case.
Realistic inputs including edge cases (typos, Hinglish, angry users, off-topic asks) with expected behaviour and the result of the last run.

length.note: Driven by how much context the model needs. Large reference data belongs in attached documents or retrieval, not pasted rules; the test set is extra.

checklist: Does it open with the role, the audience and the one job?
Are the success criteria written down, and does every rule serve one of them?
Does each rule say what to do (not only what not to do), and do non-obvious rules give a reason?
Is reference material separated from instructions with clear labels?
Is the output format specified exactly (length, structure, language, schema if parsed)?
Are there at least two varied examples, one of them an edge case?
Does it say what to do when information is missing or the request is out of scope?
Is one name used for each thing throughout?
Is it free of contradictory rules?
Is there a test set with expected behaviour and a record of the last run?
pitfalls: Shouting ('NEVER EVER do X') to fix one failure: the model can apply it too broadly. State the rule once, give the reason and add an example of the right behaviour.
Rule pile-up: each bug patched with a new line until rules contradict. Keep a changelog and re-run the whole test set after every edit.
One example the model copies word for word: vary the examples in length, topic and tone.
Shipping untested: run 20 or more real inputs, including Hinglish, typos and requests the bot must refuse.
Vague persona ('You are a world-class expert'): replace it with the concrete business context and audience.
No language rule for Indian users: specify 'reply in the user's language and script; if they write Hindi in Roman script, reply in Roman script'.
Secrets or customer data pasted into the prompt: reference them through tools or retrieval; tell the model to treat pasted documents as data, never as instructions.
Stale facts (prices, return windows) baked in: add a 'last updated' line and an owner.
cards.exemplar_brief: System prompt for 'Chai Point Bot' (fictional), the WhatsApp order-support assistant of a Bengaluru tea D2C brand: answers order status from a supplied lookup result, returns (7-day window, unopened packs only) and product questions from a 12-SKU list provided as data; customers write in English, Hindi and Hinglish; hands off to a human for refunds over Rs 2,000 and any complaint about health effects; replies under 80 words; include 3 varied examples and a 15-input test set with expected behaviour; instructions in English.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Role/audience/job up front, written success criteria each rule serves, context in labelled tags with a data-not-instructions rule, reasons on non-obvious rules, exact output format incl. script rule and a parseable [[HANDOFF]] line, 3 varied examples (Hinglish, Devanagari, health + Rs 2,000 edge), 15-input test set with expected behaviour and an honest 'not yet run' record, owner and last-updated line. Small slip: the Hinglish example mixes 'Aapka' with 'likh dena' (use 'likh dijiye').

cards.name: Tagline / slogan
cards.summary: A short line that carries a brand's promise or attitude and survives years of repetition under a logo, on packs and at the end of ads. Good lines are specific to the brand (a competitor could not sign them), easy to say aloud, and still true the hundredth time; the deliverable is a reasoned set of options with a recommendation, not one line.
use_for: Brand launches and rebrands (the line under the logo)
Campaign lines that run for one campaign
Product-range lines and pack sign-offs
Ad end cards, OOH and print sign-offs
Institution and NGO lines
avoid: Election and party slogans and chants: use genre:campaign_slogan
The brand name itself: use genre:brand_naming
Sung lines: use genre:jingle_lyrics
The internal statement of who the brand serves and how it differs: use genre:positioning_statement (write it first; the tagline compresses it)
Category-generic lines ('Quality you can trust', 'Your success, our mission'): they fail the swap test; go back to what only this brand can claim

buyers: Startups and D2C brands at launch or rebrand
Advertising and branding agencies (as part of brand identity work)
Product marketing teams needing campaign lines
cards.value_why: Fiverr's Business Names & Slogans has 1,233 gigs (2026-10-04) with Slogan and Tagline as separate deliverables and trademark-check add-ons; in India it sits inside advertising copywriting (AmbitionBox Copywriter average Rs 6.7 L a year, 2026-10-03). Few words, but priced on the thinking and the rationale.
cards.goal: The client picks one line they can own for years, and the audience repeats it and links it to the brand.

structure.does: The one thing the brand stands for, the audience, and the lines competitors already use (so the set avoids them).
Three or four territories (the promise, the attitude, the origin, the user's moment), each with a one-line rationale.
Four to six options per route, each written to be said aloud.
Each shown in context (under the logo, on the pack, as an ad end card), with why it works and its risks: trademark search needed, meaning in Hindi or regional languages.
Hindi, Hinglish or regional transcreations where the brand speaks those languages, not literal translations.

length.note: Per line. The commissioned deliverable is a set of 15-25 options plus routes and rationale, typically 300-800 words. Rhythm decides more than count.

checklist: Does each recommended line pass the swap test (a named competitor could not sign it unchanged)?
Can each line be said aloud in one breath without stumbling?
Is each line free of claims the client cannot prove ('No. 1', 'best', 'most trusted')?
Does the set cover at least three distinct routes, not twenty rewordings of one idea?
Is each recommended line shown in context with a short rationale?
Has each recommended line been checked for unintended meanings in Hindi and the brand's other languages?
Is a trademark and domain or handle availability check flagged for the shortlist?
Is the set free of category filler words (quality, trust, excellence, solutions, journey)?
pitfalls: Category cliches ('Excellence in every drop'): replace with the concrete truth only this brand has, e.g. the village mill, the 48-hour dispatch, the founder's recipe.
Puns that only work in writing: if it needs to be seen to be understood, it will not survive radio, video or word of mouth.
Unprovable superlatives ('India's most trusted'): ASCI and CCPA require substantiation for factual claims; turn them into attitude lines.
Literal Hindi translation of an English line: transcreate so the Hindi line works on its own rhythm.
Dumping 50 lines without a recommendation: clients need a reasoned top three.
A line that describes the product ('Premium cold-pressed oils') instead of the promise: that is a descriptor, keep it as a separate strapline if needed.
cards.exemplar_brief: Tagline set for 'Khet Se' (fictional), a Nashik D2C brand selling cold-pressed groundnut and mustard oils made in village wooden-press mills, sold online to urban families in Pune and Mumbai; 3 strategic routes with 5 lines each in English or Hinglish, a recommended top 3 with rationale and one Hindi (Devanagari) transcreation of each; no health or cure claims; under 600 words.

verified.note: P1 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. 3 routes x 5 lines, recap names the category cliche to avoid, top 3 in context with risks, Devanagari transcreations; the Class 29 trademark pointer and the Marathi 'ghana' / Hindi 'ghani = dense' check are correct. Writer fault: recommended #3 'Tadka that smells like home' fails the card's swap test by the writer's own admission; 'Gaon ki ghani, shehar ka tadka' from the same route was the ownable pick. 'Khet se ghani, ghani se ghar' is a strong lead line.

cards.name: Talking-head / to-camera script
cards.summary: A script for one person speaking to camera, written in that person's natural spoken voice with beats marked for cuts, B-roll and on-screen text. Good looks like a hook in the first line, one point per beat, sentences short enough to say in one breath, words the presenter actually uses, and one call to action.
use_for: Founder, doctor, CA, lawyer and coach reels on Instagram, YouTube Shorts and LinkedIn
YouTube talking-head explainers and course introduction videos
Internal CEO or leader video messages
Political and civic leader messages recorded to camera
avoid: Voice-over over stock or graphics with no face: use genre:faceless_video_script
Researched long-form YouTube videos with segments and B-roll packages: use genre:youtube_video_script
Ads performed by a creator: use genre:ugc_ad_script
Fully scripted word-for-word lines for a presenter who ad-libs: deliver bullet mode (hook and CTA verbatim, beats as bullets)

cards.value_why: Sits under Upwork's script writer type ($30-$56/hr, 2026-01-21) and under ghostwriting of video scripts; AmbitionBox puts the average Indian Script Writer at Rs 5 L a year at 1 year of experience (2026-10-03). Often sold as monthly script packs for reels.
cards.goal: The viewer watches to the end and does the one thing asked (follow, comment, book, tap the link).

structure.does: One spoken line plus matching on-screen text that names the viewer's problem or a surprising claim. No greeting, no name intro.
Why listen: one line of the presenter's experience or what the viewer loses by not knowing this.
Two to five beats, each one point with an example from the presenter's work. Mark [CUT], [B-ROLL: ...] and [TEXT: ...] cues per beat.
The takeaway restated in one line the viewer could repeat.
One action, spoken and shown on screen.

length.note: Set by the target duration: a 30-60 second reel is a short script, a 10-minute YouTube talking head a long one. Time it by reading aloud at the presenter's own pace with a stopwatch.

checklist: Does the first spoken line state the problem, claim or promise with no greeting or self-introduction?
Is every sentence sayable in one breath when read aloud?
Does it use the presenter's own words and phrases (checked against a recording of them talking)?
Is each beat one point, with a [CUT], [B-ROLL] or [TEXT] cue marked?
Are on-screen text lines shorter than the spoken lines rather than a transcript?
Is there exactly one CTA?
Does the read-aloud time match the target duration?
Are numbers written the way the presenter says them ('dedh lakh', '1.5 lakh') and checked?
For money or health topics: does it stay within the presenter's qualification, with no stock tips or cure claims?
pitfalls: 'Hi guys, welcome back to my channel' openings: cut to the hook; the intro can be a lower-third.
Written-English sentences ('Furthermore, it is imperative to note'): use contractions and the presenter's real phrasing; read it aloud and rewrite anything you stumble on.
Every word scripted for someone who ad-libs: they will sound stiff. Give them hook and CTA verbatim and the beats as bullets.
On-screen text that duplicates every spoken word: use text for the key number, term or step only.
Three CTAs at the end ('like, share, subscribe, comment, DM'): pick the one that serves the goal.
Stock-pick or 'sure-shot' tips from a finance presenter: SEBI bars regulated entities from associating with unregistered advice creators; keep it to education.
Script in Devanagari when the presenter reads a Roman-script teleprompter: ask which script they read before writing.

ban.label: dead-air opener
ban.regex: (?i)hi guys|welcome back to (my|the) channel|without further ado|in this video,? i (will|am going to)

cards.exemplar_brief: 60-second Instagram reel talking-head script for a Jaipur CA (fictional, CA Neha Agarwal, 9 years in GST practice) on '3 GST notice mistakes small traders make'; audience: kirana and textile traders in Rajasthan; Hinglish in Roman script, said the way she speaks; beats marked with [CUT], [B-ROLL] and [TEXT] cues; one CTA: comment 'NOTICE' to get her reply checklist; 130-170 spoken words.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V1 C2. 168 spoken words, no greeting, problem-first hook with matching TEXT, one credibility line from the brief only, three beats each with CUT/B-ROLL/TEXT cues, short supers, one-line payoff, one CTA (comment NOTICE). GST content is sound (reply-by date, ex parte order risk, GSTR-1 vs 3B / ITC mismatch check, documents with the reply). Writer slips: 'aapki baat suni bina' should be 'sune bina'; register swings between aap ('aapki') and tum ('dekho', 'bharoge', 'likho') inside the same 60 seconds.

cards.name: Technical blog article (developer content)
cards.summary: A marketing-blog article for engineers (code walkthrough, architecture explainer, benchmark or tool comparison) that teaches something real and earns trust for the company that publishes it. use_for: Developer-tool and SaaS company blogs (developer relations content)
Engineering-team posts on how they solved a specific problem
Tool and approach comparisons with measured results
Migration guides and feature deep-dives at launch
Guest posts on developer platforms
avoid: Documentation on a docs site: use genre:developer_tutorial, genre:api_reference or genre:readme
Internal design proposals: use genre:technical_design_doc
Generic 'What is Kubernetes' explainers written without running anything: commodity content that search engines and developers ignore; pick a narrow problem you can actually reproduce

cards.goal: The developer reader solves their problem or understands the system, and trusts the publisher enough to try the product or come back.

structure.does: Names the exact problem, the stack with versions and the outcome (e.g. 'Cut a Python Lambda cold start from 4 s to 900 ms'); who it is for and the prerequisites.
Why the problem happens (the mechanism), with a diagram or a short plain explanation.
Numbered steps, each with a language-tagged code block, what it does and the expected output.
Measured numbers with the setup (hardware, data size, versions) and how to reproduce them.
When not to use this approach and what it costs.
Summary, link to the full code, one next step (docs, repo, product trial).

length.note: Tutorials with code run longer than explainers; code blocks count. Stop when the problem is solved, not at a target count.

checklist: Does the intro name the problem, the stack with versions and the outcome?
Does every code block run as shown (tested in a clean environment), with a language tag and pinned versions?
Does each step say what the code does and what output to expect?
Are benchmark numbers given with their setup so a reader can reproduce them?
Is there a section on trade-offs or when not to use the approach?
Is the product mentioned only where it solves a step, with a non-product alternative named?
Are prerequisites listed before the first step?
Do the subheads let a reader navigate from a table of contents?
Is there a link to a repo or gist with the complete code?
pitfalls: Code written from memory that does not run: build the example in a fresh environment first, paste from the working repo, pin versions.
'Simply', 'just', 'obviously': they insult the reader who is stuck. State the step.
A sales pitch dressed as a tutorial: developers leave at the first forced product plug. Solve the problem first, mention the product once where it helps.
Screenshots of code: readers cannot copy them and search engines cannot read them; use text code blocks.
Benchmarks without setup: give hardware, data size, versions and the command used.
Undated posts against fast-moving APIs: put the date and versions near the top and update or mark them when they change.
cards.exemplar_brief: Technical blog post for a Bengaluru observability startup (fictional, 'TraceKart') on finding the slow SQL queries behind p95 latency spikes in a Django 5 + PostgreSQL 16 app using pg_stat_statements and EXPLAIN ANALYZE; audience: backend developers at Indian SaaS startups; English; 1,400-1,800 words; runnable SQL and Python snippets; product mentioned once in the wrap-up; goal: the reader fixes one slow query and tries the free tier.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Title names problem, stack with versions and outcome; prerequisites before step 1; mechanism explained (pg_stat_statements stores no percentiles, correctly said); 7 numbered steps each with tagged code and expected output. Details checked and correct: execute_wrapper signature; queryid ignores the comment so only the first view's tag is stored (stated in trade-offs); AddIndexConcurrently with atomic=False; quantiles(n=20)[18] = p95; the composite index removes the Sort node. Benchmark numbers are placeholders (brief gave none); product once in the wrap-up with the no-product path stated. Nits: the assertNumQueries snippet lacks 'from django.test import TestCase'; 'a third kind of spike' miscounts; snippets were not run (writer flagged).

cards.name: Technical specification / design doc
cards.summary: An engineer's written proposal for how a system or change will be built, reviewed before code is written. Good looks like clear context, measurable goals and stated non-goals, a design detailed enough for reviewers to find flaws, and an honest 'alternatives considered' section that explains the trade-offs behind the choice.
use_for: Design reviews for a new service, feature or migration
RFCs in open-source projects and engineering orgs
Architecture decision records (one decision per short record)
Vendor or architecture selection write-ups
Technical proposals from a development agency to a client's CTO
avoid: What users need and why (requirements, not the build): use genre:prd
A step-by-step implementation manual with no trade-offs: Ubl's advice is that the program itself would have been a better use of time
Explaining the system to outside developers for marketing: use genre:technical_blog_article
Tiny changes a code review can cover: no doc needed

sources.title: Design Docs at Google (Malte Ubl), read 2026-10-05
sources.supports: sections: 'Context and scope', 'Goals and non-goals', 'The actual design', 'Alternatives considered', 'Cross-cutting concerns'; 'The sweet spot for a larger project seems to be around 10-20ish pages'; a '1-3 page mini design doc' for incremental improvements; docs that are 'really implementation manuals' without trade-offs are a sign no doc was needed; reviews range from comment threads to formal design review meetings

buyers: Engineering teams and tech leads (usually written in-house)
Software development agencies proposing a build to a client
cards.value_why: An internal engineering artefact written by the engineers who will build the system; outside paid work is mostly editing engineers' drafts or agency proposals, though it sits in well-paid technical writing (BLS median $90,390 for technical writers, May 2025).
cards.goal: Reviewers can approve, reject or improve the design before code is written, and future engineers can see why it was built this way.

structure.does: Title, author, reviewers, status (draft, in review, approved, superseded), date, links to tickets.
What exists today, the problem, constraints, and a system-context diagram or described flow.
Bulleted, measurable goals ('p99 under 200 ms at 5,000 requests per second'); non-goals that a reasonable reader might assume are included but are not.
Architecture, APIs, data model and storage, key flows and failure handling, with diagrams; detailed enough that a reviewer can spot a flaw.
Two or three real alternatives, each with the specific trade-off that ruled it out.
Security, privacy (personal data under DPDP for Indian users), observability, cost, rollout, migration and rollback.
Unresolved questions with owners; decisions made during review with dates.

length.note: Pages. A 1-3 page mini design doc for incremental changes, about 10-20 pages for a larger project (Ubl). An ADR fits on one page: context, decision, consequences.

checklist: Does the header show status, author, reviewers and date?
Are the goals measurable, and are non-goals stated?
Is there at least one diagram or a described data or request flow?
Are at least two alternatives described with the specific reason each was rejected?
Does it cover security, privacy, observability, cost, rollout and rollback?
Is the design detailed enough (APIs, data model, failure modes) for a reviewer to find a flaw?
Are open questions listed with owners?
Is the length proportionate (a mini doc for an increment, a fuller doc for a new system)?
Is the hardest part of the problem designed in detail rather than waved through ('we will just cache it')?
pitfalls: An implementation manual with no trade-offs: if there is nothing to decide, skip the doc and write the code.
Strawman alternatives nobody would pick: include the option a senior colleague would actually argue for, and say honestly why it lost.
Vague goals ('fast', 'scalable'): give a number, a load and a percentile.
Hand-waving the hard part: name the failure modes (timeouts, duplicates, partial writes) and how each is handled.
A doc frozen after review while the build changes: update status and the decision log; supersede ADRs with a new record rather than editing the old one.
Skipping personal data: list what personal data the system stores, why, for how long and who can read it.
cards.exemplar_brief: Mini design doc (900-1,300 words, 2-3 pages) for a Pune fintech's (fictional, 'PaySetu') move from nightly batch to near-real-time UPI settlement reconciliation using Kafka; audience: the engineering team and the CTO reviewing it; English; must include header, goals and non-goals, the design with one described flow, two alternatives considered (polling the bank's API; a managed change-data-capture tool), cross-cutting concerns including the personal data involved, rollout and rollback.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Header with status/reviewers/date (7 and 14 Oct 2026 are Wednesdays, correct), measurable goals and real non-goals, one numbered flow (outbox -> Kafka keyed by RRN -> idempotent upsert), failure handling for duplicates, crashes, poison messages, webhook outage and late credits; two honest alternatives with the specific reason each lost (polling latency floor; CDC schema coupling and WAL retention); DPDP and the RBI 6 April 2018 data-localisation circular correctly cited and marked for compliance; rollout, rollback flag, open questions with owners. Flaw a reviewer will catch: nothing fires UNMATCHED_TIMEOUT when no second event arrives (needs a scheduled sweeper or timer topic).

cards.name: TED-style talk
cards.summary: A short talk built around one idea worth spreading, carried by a throughline of story and evidence. Good looks like an opening that earns attention, the idea stated plainly early on, every story and statistic building that one idea, and an ending that shows the audience what they can now see or do; no selling from the stage.
use_for: TEDx talks
Idea-led conference talks and short keynote slots without a product pitch
Indian talk formats in the same mould (college fests, community talk platforms)
Internal company idea talks
avoid: Company events where the product, roadmap or results are the point: use genre:keynote_speech
Rally-style talks built on emotion more than an idea: use genre:motivational_speech
Political platforms: use genre:political_speech (TEDx rules bar talks with an inflammatory political or religious agenda)
Promoting the speaker's own products, books or business: TEDx rules forbid it; move it to the speaker's bio or website

sources.title: TED: TEDx rules (read 2026-10-05)
sources.supports: 'TEDx talks are typically under 18 minutes'; 'Many talks are even shorter, with 3-9 minutes being ideal for a focused idea'; 'Speakers cannot promote their own products, books, or businesses, or those of a company which employs them'; 'No talks with an inflammatory political or religious agenda, nor polarizing us vs them language'; 'Scientific claims by speakers should be based on data that has survived scrutiny by experts in the field'; 'TEDx events may neither pay nor charge speakers'

sources.title: Upwork: 14 Types of Freelance Writing Jobs and What They Pay (published 2026-01-21)
sources.supports: ghostwriters charge $20-$45 per hour on Upwork

buyers: TEDx speakers: founders, doctors, academics, athletes, social entrepreneurs
Speaker coaches who bring in a writer
PR agencies preparing executives for stage appearances
Students and young professionals selected for TEDx or college events
cards.value_why: TEDx events run worldwide and speakers hire coaches and writers; because TEDx may neither pay nor charge speakers, the speaker or their company pays for the script (ghostwriting rates, Upwork $20-$45/hr band, 2026-01-21).
cards.goal: The audience leaves able to state the speaker's one idea in a sentence and with a reason to act on it.

structure.does: A specific moment, image, object or question that creates curiosity. No thanks, no self-introduction.
The problem or stakes for this audience, in their terms.
Stated in one plain sentence the audience could repeat.
Two to four steps, each a story or piece of evidence that adds to the idea (not a string of anecdotes), with the strongest objection answered.
What the audience can now see, try or decide differently.
Returns to the opening image and restates the idea in its final form.

length.note: TEDx talks are typically under 18 minutes, with 3-9 minutes ideal for a focused idea (TEDx rules). Write to the organiser's slot and time it by rehearsing aloud at the speaker's pace.

checklist: Can the idea be stated in one sentence, and is it stated plainly by the end of the first third?
Does the opening start with a specific moment, image or question rather than thanks or a self-introduction?
Does every story or statistic connect explicitly to the idea?
Is it free of any pitch for the speaker's or employer's products, books or business?
Are scientific claims backed by data experts accept, with sources kept in the speaker notes?
Is it free of 'us versus them' political or religious framing?
Does the rehearsed time fit the organiser's slot?
Does the ending return to the opening and tell the audience what they can now see or do?
Is every technical term explained through something the audience already knows?
pitfalls: The life story as a talk (a spoken CV in chronological order): pick the one idea and keep only the stories that build it.
Three ideas in one talk: the audience remembers none. Cut to one and move the rest to another talk.
Written-English sentences the speaker stumbles on: rehearse aloud and rewrite every line that trips.
Pitching from the stage ('my book, available on Amazon'): it breaks TEDx rules and loses the room.
An inspirational ending with no idea behind it ('follow your dreams'): end on the specific shift the talk argued for.
Unchecked statistics and pseudoscience: TEDx asks for data that has survived expert scrutiny; cite the study in the notes or cut the claim.

ban.label: thank-you opener, stage pitch or empty ending
ban.regex: (?i)thank you (so much )?for having me|it'?s an honou?r to be here|follow your (dreams|passion)|buy my|available on amazon

cards.exemplar_brief: 8-minute TEDx talk script (about 1,000-1,150 words) for a Patna government-school maths teacher (fictional, Ranjana Kumari) whose idea is 'children fail maths because we teach it in a language they do not dream in': she began explaining in Bhojpuri-Hindi and her class's Class 10 maths pass rate rose from 54% to 81% over three years (her school's records, supplied); audience: a TEDx event at a Patna college; English with natural Hindi and Bhojpuri lines; no product, book or coaching mention.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C2. Opens on an audience exercise (seven eights, then the same field problem in textbook Hindi and in Bhojpuri), idea stated plainly in the first third, building steps (market maths vs textbook word, samikaran as a balance scale, the 54% -> 81% records with honest limits), strongest objection ('the exam is not in Bhojpuri') answered, a concrete ask for non-teachers, close returns to seven eights and restates the idea. Natural Bhojpuri lines (ego khet ba, ketna taar laagi, bujhail). NEP 2020 home-language point correct (para 4.11) and marked verify. One check for the speaker: the chanted table is usually 'saat atthe chhappan' (written here as 'aathe').

cards.name: Telegram channel post
cards.summary: A broadcast message to a Telegram channel's subscribers (news, a deal, a class update, a job alert, a lesson) formatted for a phone with the news in the first line, short blocks and one link. Good looks like a post a subscriber can act on from the notification preview, in the channel's consistent format, with nothing that reads as unregistered investment advice or a fake deadline.
use_for: Coaching and exam-prep channels (UPSC, SSC, state exams): class schedules, notes, mock tests
Deal, coupon and affiliate channels
News, job-alert and government-scheme update channels
Creator and brand announcement channels
Finance and markets education channels (education only)
avoid: WhatsApp Channels: use genre:whatsapp_channel_post (different formatting and reach)
Paid sponsored messages: write them to plat:telegram_ads limits
Replies inside a group discussion: use genre:community_post
Buy or sell calls, target prices and 'sure-shot' tips: unregistered investment advice; SEBI-regulated firms may not associate with creators who give it. Teach concepts instead

sources.supports: message text '1-4096 characters after entities parsing'

sources.title: Telegram Bot API: sendPhoto
sources.supports: photo caption '0-1024 characters after entities parsing'

cards.value_why: No dedicated marketplace category found on 2026-10-04; channel owners write their own or it is bundled with community management.
cards.goal: The subscriber reads the post and takes the one action (opens the link, joins the live class, applies, buys) without muting the channel.

structure.does: The news or offer in bold, readable on its own because it is what the notification preview shows. One emoji only if the channel uses them.
Two to six short lines or bullets: date, time, price, deadline, eligibility, what changed.
One link with descriptive text, or a button, telling the reader exactly what happens when they tap.
Series tag for search inside the channel, source for news, disclaimer where the topic needs one.

length.note: Hard ceilings: 4,096 characters for a text message and 1,024 for a media caption from a non-Premium account, counted after formatting is parsed. Most good channel posts are far shorter; split long content into a series.

checklist: Does the first line state the news or offer on its own?
Is it within 4,096 characters (text message) or 1,024 (media caption, non-Premium sender)?
Are the key facts (date, time, price, deadline, eligibility) in the first few lines?
Is there exactly one primary link or action?
Does formatting use Telegram's native bold, italic and link entities rather than raw Markdown symbols showing in the preview?
For news: is the source named?
For finance: is it free of buy or sell calls, target prices and guaranteed returns?
For coaching: are result claims (ranks, selections) true and not misleading?
Is any deadline or scarcity real?
pitfalls: A wall of text: break it into two-to-four-line blocks with the key fact in bold.
Emoji on every line: one at the start, if the channel style uses them, is enough.
Stock 'calls' and 'jackpot' tips: rewrite as an explainer on the concept, or do not post.
Link-only posts: say what the link is and why to open it now.
Coaching posts claiming toppers who were not your students or hiding the course they took: the CCPA coaching guidelines target exactly this.
Raw Markdown asterisks showing when posting through a bot: set the parse mode and check the preview before sending.
Real-money gaming promotions: advertising online money games is banned under the 2025 Act; decline the post.
cards.exemplar_brief: Telegram channel post for 'Rajasthan Patwari Prep' (fictional coaching channel, 40,000 subscribers) announcing a free full-length live mock test on Sunday at 8 pm, followed by an answer-key session at 10 pm; audience: Rajasthan Patwari exam aspirants; Hinglish in Roman script with key Hindi terms; under 90 words; one join link; no selection-guarantee claims.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V1 C1. First line works as the notification preview, date added correctly (Sunday 11 October 2026), times and the answer-key session in the first lines, one tag, one link, no selection claim, ~62 words. Writer faults: the action line 'Join karein: [join link]' does not say what tapping does (opens the live test? sets a reminder?); register mixes 'hal karo' with 'Join karein'.

cards.name: Testimonial collection & testimonial page copy
cards.summary: Two linked jobs: the request and question set that draws specific, quotable customer stories, and the testimonials or reviews page built from them. Good testimonials name a real person (with consent), their situation before, a specific result and a detail only a real customer would know, edited for length and clarity but never for meaning.
use_for: Testimonial and reviews pages on service, SaaS and D2C websites
Proof blocks for landing and sales pages
Interview scripts for video testimonials
Pull quotes for decks, brochures and case studies
Review-request messages after a purchase or project
avoid: The full story with process and metrics: use genre:case_study

Writing testimonials for customers to sign, or generating them with AI: the FTC's 2024 rule bans fake and AI-generated reviews and CCPA requires endorsements to reflect genuine opinion. Interview real customers instead
Paid creator content: use genre:sponsored_creator_post with disclosure

sources.title: Fiverr: Website Content subcategory
sources.supports: page search data on 2026-10-04: 4310 gigs; page-type filter includes Reviews and Testimonials

sources.title: AWAI: 80 In-Demand Copywriting Projects (updated 2026-02-02)
sources.supports: lists Testimonial as a copywriting project type with its own fee guideline

sources.title: CCPA Guidelines for Prevention of Misleading Advertisements and Endorsements, 2022
sources.supports: endorsements must reflect the endorser's genuine, reasonably current opinion based on adequate experience; material connections must be disclosed (cl. 13-14)

buyers: Service businesses: clinics, coaches, CA and law firms, agencies
B2B sales teams needing quotes for decks
cards.value_why: Fiverr's Website Content lists Testimonials and Reviews as page types and AWAI lists Testimonial as a project, but it is usually a small add-on to website or case-study work.
cards.goal: A prospect reading the page sees someone like them who got the result, and believes it.

structure.does: Short, personal ask: why, how long it takes, how it will be used, and the consent question.
Five to seven open questions: what was going on before, what almost stopped you, why you chose us, one moment that stood out, the result (number or time), who you would recommend it to.
Written permission for name, photo, company or city, and approval of the edited quote before it goes live.
Who these customers are and what they came for, in one or two lines.
Two or three longer testimonials with name, role or city and photo; the specific result pulled out as a highlighted line.
Grouped by use case or by the objection they answer (price, time, trust).
One next step after the proof.

length.note: Driven by how many usable testimonials exist. Fewer real, specific quotes beat a long wall of vague praise.

checklist: Is every quote traceable to a real customer's own words on file (recording, email, form)?
Has each customer approved the edited version and consented to the use of their name and photo?
Does each featured testimonial include a before situation and a specific result?
Is each attributed with a name plus role, company or city?
Are employees, relatives and customers who received anything for the review disclosed as such?
Are exceptional results presented without implying every customer gets them?
Are short quotes grouped by the objection or use case they answer?
Does the question set ask for specifics (numbers, moments, hesitations) rather than 'How was your experience?'
Is there one CTA after the proof?
pitfalls: Rewriting quotes into marketing copy ('This revolutionary service transformed my business'): keep the customer's words, cut for length, fix grammar only, and get approval.
Inventing or AI-generating testimonials, even 'representative' ones: illegal under the FTC rule and misleading under CCPA. If you have no testimonials yet, use other proof.
'Rahul S., Delhi' with nothing specific: ask for role, photo and one concrete detail, or it reads as fake.
Generic questions that get generic praise: ask 'What almost stopped you from booking?' and 'What changed in the first month?'
Hindi or Hinglish testimonials polished into formal English: keep the original words, add a translation if the page is English.
Hiding that a reviewer got a free product or discount: disclose it next to the quote.
cards.exemplar_brief: Testimonial kit and page for a Jaipur physiotherapy clinic (fictional, 'MoveWell Physio') that treats desk-job back pain: (1) a WhatsApp request message in Hinglish asking recent patients for a testimonial, with consent wording; (2) a 6-question interview set; (3) a testimonials page built only from the four patient notes below, inventing nothing beyond them; page in English; under 700 words in total; no cure claims. DEMO DATA: the clinic, the patients and their words are invented for this test assignment; all four gave written approval of the edited quote and consent to first name, age and job (no photos); present every result as an individual result. Note 1: Ankit, 34, software tester, could not sit for 30 minutes, back to a full workday in 5 weeks. Quote: "I used to stand up every 20 minutes. By week five I worked a full day and forgot to watch the clock." Note 2: Meenal, 41, chartered accountant, back pain that ran down her left leg, slept through the night again after 3 weeks. Quote: "I had stopped saying yes to dinners because sitting hurt. In the third week I slept through the night." Note 3: Rohit, 29, call-centre team leader, stiff neck and daily headaches, headaches down to about once a week after 8 sessions. Quote: "I came for my neck. The headaches going down to once a week was the bonus." Note 4: Sunita, 52, school accountant, back pain during month-end closing, walking to school again after 6 weeks; she nearly did not book because she expected hot packs and waiting. Quote: "They gave me three exercises I could do at my desk. In six weeks I was walking to school again."

verified.note: P1 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. The WhatsApp ask is natural Hinglish with clear consent and no-penalty-for-refusal wording; 6 specific questions incl. 'what almost stopped you'; consent split four ways with approval before publishing and a disclosure rule; the page has one CTA and an individual-results line, no cure claim. The page itself is three-quarters placeholders because the brief supplied only one of the 'four supplied patient notes'; the writer correctly invented nothing. CARD FIX: exemplar_brief -> include all four patient notes verbatim (three more like 'Ankit, 34, software tester, could not sit for 30 minutes, back to a full workday in 5 weeks', each with a short quote in the patient's own words) instead of 'four supplied patient notes (e.g. ...)' with one given. | CARD FIXED 2026-10-07 (fix_genre_d): exemplar_brief now carries all four patient notes with a short quote each, consent and individual-result rule (demo data); re-judge pending.

cards.name: Thesis summary / PhD synopsis
cards.summary: A condensed account of a thesis (problem, objectives, method, findings and contribution to knowledge) in the format a university's ordinance prescribes, submitted at registration (as a research proposal) or at thesis submission. Good looks like a precisely stated research gap, numbered objectives that each map to a finding, specific methods, findings with numbers, and an explicit claim of what is new.
use_for: PhD registration synopsis presented to the research or departmental committee
Pre-submission synopsis sent ahead of the thesis
Summaries for external examiners and the viva
Extended research summaries for fellowship, postdoc or faculty applications
avoid: A 150-300 word journal or conference abstract: use genre:research_abstract
The literature chapter: use genre:literature_review
Writing the research itself for the scholar: academic misconduct; work only as an editor of the scholar's own design and findings
Inventing results to fill the findings section at registration: write expected outcomes in the future tense instead

sources.title: EFA 2026 Rate Chart (1,100+ member survey, Nov 2025-Jan 2026)
sources.supports: Ghostwriting > Scientific '$72.50-$188.00' per hour; Technical '$75.00-$126.00' per hour (academic and scientific writing rates)

buyers: PhD scholars seeking editing and structuring help
Masters students with a dissertation summary requirement
cards.value_why: Required by Indian universities in the PhD process but rarely an open-market commission; paid work is mostly academic editing, which the EFA 2026 chart prices at scientific-writing hourly rates.
cards.goal: The committee or examiner understands what was studied, how, what was found and what is new, and approves registration or submission.

structure.does: Title, scholar, supervisor, department, university and year, exactly as the ordinance prescribes.
The field, the problem and why it matters, narrowing quickly to the specific question.

structure.part: Review of literature and research gap
structure.does: The key prior studies grouped by theme, ending in one or two sentences that state precisely what is not yet known.
Numbered, each specific enough to be answered by the method.
Design, population and sample (size, selection), tools and instruments, analysis methods, ethics approval.
One short paragraph per chapter saying what it covers.
At submission: key findings with numbers and the direction of each effect, mapped to the objectives. At registration: expected outcomes in the future tense.
What the work adds to knowledge or practice, stated explicitly; its limits and suggested further research.
Every cited work, in the one style the department uses.

length.note: Set by each university's ordinance (page or word limits, headings, sometimes the language); check the current ordinance before drafting. A registration synopsis is usually shorter than a submission synopsis.

checklist: Does it follow the university's prescribed headings, order and length?
Is the research gap stated in one or two sentences that point to the specific prior work it builds on?
Are objectives numbered, and does each map to a finding (or an expected outcome at registration)?
Is the method specific: design, sample size and selection, tools, analysis?
Are findings stated with numbers and the direction of effect?
Is the contribution to knowledge stated explicitly and only as far as the findings support?
Are limitations stated?
Are all references in one consistent style and cited in the text?
Is the tense right: future for planned work at registration, past for what was done at submission?
pitfalls: Background bloat with thin findings: cap the introduction and put the space into results and contribution.

A vague contribution ('This study will be useful to policymakers'): say what is now known that was not, e.g. 'the first district-level estimate of UPI acceptance among kirana retailers in western Rajasthan'.
Objectives that do not match the findings: build a two-column table (objective, finding) and fix any orphan.
Literature pasted from sources: similarity-check software will flag it; summarise in your own words and cite.
Methods written as a textbook definition ('Survey research is a method that...'): describe what this study did.
Ghostwriting results or analysis for the scholar: refuse; edit language and structure only.
cards.exemplar_brief: Pre-submission PhD synopsis (2,000-2,500 words) for a commerce scholar at a Rajasthan state university (fictional): 'Adoption of UPI among kirana retailers in Jodhpur district', mixed methods, survey of 400 retailers plus 20 interviews; supplied findings: 71% accept UPI daily, fear of settlement delays and rumours about transaction charges are the main barriers, adoption is 2x higher where a family member under 30 runs the counter; English; headings: introduction, review and gap, objectives, methodology, chapter scheme, findings, contribution and limitations, references.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp1 V2 C2. All eight prescribed headings in order, past tense for done work, five numbered objectives each mapped to a finding in an at-a-glance list, hypothesis for objective 3, method specific where the brief allowed, contribution limited to what the findings support, association-not-causation limit stated. References checked and correct (Davis 1989 MISQ 13(3) 319-340; Venkatesh et al. 2003 27(3) 425-478; Venkatesh, Thong & Xu 2012 36(1) 157-178; Rogers 2003 5th ed.; Creswell & Plano Clark 2018 3rd ed.). Heavy but legitimate placeholders (Indian literature, sampling frame, test statistics), since the card forbids ghostwriting results.

Good looks like a claim a reasonable expert could disagree with, proof from the author's own operations, the strongest objection answered, and recommendations readers can act on.
use_for: LinkedIn articles and newsletter editions by founders and CXOs
Bylined pieces for Indian business and trade media
Point-of-view pieces on a company blog
Essays that back a conference talk or a sales conversation
avoid: Generic trend roundups ('5 trends shaping fintech in 2026'): that is commodity content with no author behind it; find the claim first
Short posts: use genre:ghostwritten_founder_post or genre:linkedin_post
Newspaper op-ed pages with their own rules: use genre:opinion_column
Research-heavy gated reports: use genre:white_paper
Placed articles written to a publication's editorial brief: use genre:byline_article

structure.does: States the claim, not the topic ('Indian SMB SaaS will be won on WhatsApp, not in the app store', not 'The future of SaaS').
The claim plus the tension: what most people in the industry believe and why the author disagrees.
Two or three proofs only this author has: their own numbers, a decision they made and what happened, a customer pattern they have seen (with permission).
The best counter-argument stated fairly, then answered.
What readers should do differently, as specific steps.
The claim restated in a line people can quote, plus an invitation to respond.

length.note: Long enough to prove one claim; trade-media bylines often set their own limit. Cut any section that does not move the argument.

checklist: Can the central claim be stated in one sentence that a reasonable expert could disagree with?
Is the claim in the headline or first paragraph?
Are there at least two pieces of evidence only this author has (own data, a decision, a client pattern shared with permission)?
Is the strongest counter-argument stated fairly and answered?
Does it end with specific recommendations?
Has the named author confirmed they would say every sentence in a meeting?
Is every third-party number attributed to its publisher and year?
Is it free of generic trend filler and of a pitch for the company's product?
pitfalls: Commodity trend commentary that any company could publish: interview the author until you find the thing they believe that peers do not, then build only on that.
Hedging every sentence ('may', 'could potentially'): commit to the claim and put the honest caveats in the objection section.
The ghostwriter's voice, not the author's: record a 30-45 minute interview, use their phrases and stories, and run an approval round.
A product pitch in disguise: readers and editors spot it; mention the company only as the source of the evidence.
Unattributed statistics ('studies show'): name the study and year, or use the author's own data.
Confidential client details: anonymise or get written permission before publishing.

ban.label: generic trend filler
ban.regex: (?i)in today'?s (fast-paced|digital|ever-changing) world|\bgame[- ]changer\b|paradigm shift|the future is (here|now)|it'?s no secret that

cards.exemplar_brief: LinkedIn article under the name of the founder of a Coimbatore textile-machinery spare-parts maker (fictional, 'Kovai Precision', Rs 80 crore revenue, 22 years in business) arguing that Indian MSME manufacturers should win domestic replacement demand before chasing export orders; supplied evidence: domestic repeat-order rate 68% against 22% for export buyers, and a 2023 export order that locked up six months of working capital; audience: MSME owners and plant heads; English; 1,000-1,300 words; goal: comments and DMs from manufacturers.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Claim in headline and opening, tension named (export-or-stay-small advice), two proofs only this author has (68% vs 22% repeat rate, translated correctly to about 2 of 3 vs 2 of 9; the 2023 order that locked up six months of working capital), a fair risk-diversification objection answered on working capital, five concrete steps, a quotable close plus an invitation to comment or DM. 1,087 words, no pitch, no unattributed stats. Placeholders where the founder must supply the decision taken after 2023.

cards.name: Threads post
cards.summary: A short conversational text post on Meta's Threads, written to start replies rather than to broadcast. Good looks like one opinion, observation or question in a human voice, under the 500-character limit, with one topic tag at most and an open end that invites people to answer.
use_for: Brand voice presence for consumer and D2C brands
Creators extending reach from Instagram
Founders' informal takes and questions to their audience
Community questions and polls of opinion
Reworking a LinkedIn or X idea into a conversational post
avoid: X-style hashtag strings and link-dump posts: Threads uses one topic tag per post
Formal announcements: use genre:linkedin_post or genre:press_release
Long multi-post monologues: if it needs more than a few self-replies, it is a genre:x_thread or a carousel
Paid promotions without the partnership label: use genre:sponsored_creator_post rules

cards.goal: Readers reply or quote the post, and the conversation brings profile visits and follows.

structure.does: The opinion, observation or question; often the whole post. Must make sense on its own in the feed.
One specific detail, example or number that makes the point concrete.
A question or an unfinished take that invites a reply, phrased as the voice would naturally ask it.
One topic tag where it helps discovery; an image only if it adds to the joke or point.

length.note: 500 characters per post (Meta developer docs). Many of the best posts are one or two lines; self-replies can continue a thought when needed.

checklist: Is each post under 500 characters?
Does it make one point or ask one question?
Does the first line work on its own in the feed?
Does it invite replies with a real question or an open take rather than 'comment below'?
Is there at most one topic tag and no hashtag string?
Does it read like a person talking, not an ad?
Is any paid partnership labelled?
If the brand jokes about a topic, is it free of punching down at people or communities?
pitfalls: Cross-posting from X with hashtags and @handles that do not exist on Threads: rewrite natively.
Broadcast announcements ('We are excited to announce'): find the conversational angle, e.g. ask what people would use it for.
Engagement bait ('Reply YES if you agree'): it draws low-value replies; ask something people have an actual opinion on.
Brand banter about tragedies, religion or politics: skip it; the conversation will not stay friendly.
Ten-post monologues: if the idea needs that much room, make it a carousel or article and post the sharpest line here.

ban.label: broadcast or bait phrasing
ban.regex: (?i)we are (thrilled|excited) to announce|reply yes if|comment below|link in bio

cards.exemplar_brief: Three standalone Threads posts for a Pune filter-coffee D2C brand (fictional, 'Kaapi Katta') in its witty, slightly nerdy voice, for 22-35-year-old urban coffee drinkers: one opinion post, one question post and one observation about office chai-versus-coffee culture; Hinglish in Roman script where natural; each under 400 characters; at most one topic tag each; no discount push.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Three standalone posts at 305/253/257 chars, one tag max each, no brand push. The witty-nerdy voice lands ('after hot milk and sugar have had their say', 'Pouring from a height counts as technique'); post 3's Hinglish office observation (chai drinkers go in groups, coffee drinkers alone) is natural and ends on a real question. Post 1 ends as a take rather than an open question, acceptable as an 'unpopular opinion'.

cards.name: Topic cluster (spoke) article
cards.summary: A focused article that answers one subtopic or long-tail question completely and links up to its pillar page and across to sibling articles. Good looks like an intent the pillar does not already answer, the answer in the first paragraph, more depth on that one question than the pillar gives, first-hand detail, and descriptive internal links.
use_for: SEO content programmes sold as batches of supporting articles
Filling gaps found in a cluster map or content audit
Supporting a pillar for SaaS, fintech, D2C, health or education sites
Long-tail Hindi and Hinglish queries
avoid: The broad overview: use genre:pillar_page
Templated pages generated at scale from data: use genre:programmatic_seo_page
A single short question: use genre:faq_answer_article
A spoke that repeats a pillar section: the two pages compete for the same query; merge or re-angle

cards.goal: The searcher with this exact question gets a complete answer, then clicks to the pillar or a sibling for the next step.

structure.does: Title with the long-tail query front-loaded; meta description that answers it in brief.
Answers the query outright so it can stand alone as a snippet or AI citation, with the pillar linked in or right after it.
H2s for the follow-up questions real searchers ask (People Also Ask, forums, sales calls), each opening with a direct answer sentence, then steps, examples and numbers.
The expert's example, photo, test result, screenshot or worked case that a rewrite of other pages could not produce.
Links to two to four sibling articles where the reader's next question is answered, and one CTA (pillar, lead magnet or product).

length.note: Intent sets length: a how-to with steps runs longer than a definition. Do not pad to match competitors' word counts.

checklist: Does it target one query and intent that neither the pillar nor another sibling already answers in full (checked against the cluster map)?
Is the query answered in the first 80 words?
Does it link to the pillar early with descriptive anchor text?
Does it link to at least two siblings where the reader's next question is answered?
Does each H2 open with a direct answer sentence?
Is there at least one first-hand element (own test, photo, data, expert quote)?
Are facts, prices and rules dated and sourced?
Is the main query in the first half of the title?
Is it free of filler intros ('In this article we will')?
pitfalls: Cannibalisation: two spokes, or a spoke and the pillar, chasing one intent. Check the cluster map first; merge duplicates and redirect.
A spoke that rehashes the pillar's overview: go one level deeper on the narrow question instead.
Orphan spokes with no links in or out: add the link from the pillar too, not only to it.
'Click here' and 'read more' anchors: use the target's topic as the anchor ('how to season a cast-iron kadai').
Padding to a competitor's word count: answer completely, then stop.
Batches of AI-drafted spokes with nothing first-hand: Google's scaled-content abuse policy targets this; add the expert's own detail to every piece.

ban.label: filler intro or vague anchor
ban.regex: (?i)in this (article|blog|post),? (we will|we'll|you will learn)|click here|without further ado

cards.exemplar_brief: Spoke article for a Coimbatore cast-iron cookware D2C brand (fictional, 'Kalchatti Co.'); pillar: 'Cast iron cookware: the complete guide'; target query: 'how to remove rust from cast iron tawa'; audience: home cooks in Indian cities with their first cast-iron tawa; English with Hindi and Tamil kitchen terms where natural; 900-1,200 words; answer in the first 80 words; link up to the pillar and across to the siblings 'How to season a cast iron kadai' and 'Cast iron vs non-stick for dosa'; one CTA to the brand's seasoning oil.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C0. Query answered in the first ~70 words with the pillar linked right after, every H2 opens with a direct answer, both siblings linked with descriptive anchors, sensible vinegar-soak limits and re-seasoning steps, natural Hindi/Tamil terms (uppu, elumichai, nallennai, dosa kal), dated. The first-hand block is a placeholder (brief supplied no test). Writer fault: the oil section says 'pick one you already have... the oil matters less than the thinness', which undercuts the single CTA to the brand's seasoning oil one section later; 'inside, outside' is odd for a flat tawa.

cards.name: Topical / moment-marketing ad
cards.summary: A fast brand reaction to news, a match, a festival or a viral moment: one witty line (often a pun, often Hinglish) plus one visual that ties the moment to the brand while people are still talking about it. Good looks like a joke understood in two seconds, a link to the brand that would not work for any other brand, and nothing that mocks tragedy, takes political sides or borrows someone's fame without rights.
use_for: Daily or weekly topicals in Indian agency social retainers
Cricket and sports moments
Festivals, Budget day, space launches, award nights
Viral memes and trends adapted for a brand
Print and hoarding topicals in the long-running Amul style
avoid: Tragedies, disasters, deaths and communal incidents: skip them or post a sincere, unbranded message
Partisan political jokes for a commercial brand: even Amul's topicals have drawn party pressure and withdrawals; brands with no political mandate should stay out
Long-form reactions (blogs, PR pitches) to news: use genre:newsjacking_post
Using a celebrity's, player's or leader's photo or name as if they endorse the brand: use the brand's own mascot, product and wordplay

buyers: Indian FMCG and D2C brands' social teams
Advertising and social agencies on monthly retainers
Startups in food delivery, fintech and consumer apps
Local businesses with an active social presence
cards.value_why: Indian agency social retainers routinely include topicals (harvest note, qualitative; no market list found); the format has a long Indian lineage through Amul's topicals since 1967.
cards.goal: The audience gets the joke in two seconds, smiles or shares it, and remembers which brand made it.

structure.does: What happened, when, the public mood, and risks: tragedy, politics, religion, a sub judice case, a person who has not consented.
The one link between the moment and the brand's product or truth.
The pun or twist, readable on a phone thumbnail.
One image idea using the product, packaging or mascot; no real-person photos or official marks without rights.
Adds context if needed and signs off with the brand, without explaining the joke.
Three to five routes per moment so approval is fast.

length.note: Per topical: the line plus the caption. Speed matters more than length; the set of options and visual notes is extra. Lint the whole option sheet against the 600-word cap (five options plus visual directions); check each option's headline line + caption (3-40 words) separately.

checklist: Will it publish while the moment is still being discussed (same day for news and matches)?
Can the line be understood in about two seconds without the caption?
Would the joke fail if another brand's name were swapped in?
Is it free of tragedy, communal, caste and partisan angles?
Does it avoid implying endorsement by a real person or team, and avoid national emblems and the names or images of national leaders?
Does it avoid using a competitor's mark to mock it?
If it is a pun, does it work in both languages it mixes?
Are there at least three options for approval?
Is the caption short, with no more than two hashtags?
pitfalls: Reacting to a rail accident, a death or a riot with a brand joke: the backlash outlasts the post. Post nothing, or a sincere message without the product.
Arriving a day late: a topical lives for hours; keep pre-approved templates and a fast approval chain.
A forced bridge ('Chandrayaan landed, and so did our new mattress'): if the link needs explaining, drop the moment.
Official tournament marks, player photos and broadcast frames: these need licences; use the brand's own visuals and let the words carry the reference.
Punching down at a person or community for a laugh: aim the joke at the situation.
Explaining the joke in the caption: trust the audience; the caption adds the brand, not the punchline.
cards.exemplar_brief: Five topical options for a Bengaluru filter-coffee D2C brand (fictional, 'Kaapi Kudi') reacting the same day to heavy rain that stalls the city's traffic for hours; for Instagram and X; each option = one headline line in English or Hinglish under 10 words, a one-line visual direction using the brand's steel tumbler-and-dabara, and a caption under 30 words; no mockery of named officials, no real-person photos.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C0. Moment check with a clear skip rule (deaths, flooded homes, rescues), one bridge, five options each with line, tumbler-and-dabara visual and short caption; no officials, junctions or real people. Best lines: 'Gaadi nahi chal rahi? Kaapi toh chalegi.' and the dobara/dabara pun. Option 1 ('boond, boond, gaadi') needs more than two seconds, and option 4, the clearest, is left out of the recommended pair. The whole-file lint failure is the card's, not the piece's. CARD FIX: lint.max_words -> raise from 150 to 600, since the card's length note says 3-40 words is per option and the exemplar asks for five options plus visual directions; check each option's line + caption separately. | CARD FIXED 2026-10-07 (fix_genre_d): lint.max_words 150 -> 600; length note says to check each option's line + caption separately; re-judge pending.

cards.name: Trade show / exhibition materials
cards.summary: The words on and around an expo booth: back-wall headline, standees and banners, product labels, the staff opener, the leave-behind handout and the follow-up email. Good looks like a back-wall line that says who you serve and what you do from across the aisle, panels read in seconds like outdoor ads, detail moved to the handout, and staff who open with a qualifying question.
use_for: Industrial and engineering expos (machine tools, auto components, packaging)
SaaS and technology conference booths
Education fairs and study-abroad expos
Real estate, franchise and consumer expos
Export trade fairs with international visitors
avoid: The full product brochure: use genre:brochure_copy and hand it out
Roadside hoardings: use genre:ooh_billboard_copy
Pre-event invitations and promotion: use genre:event_promotion
Multi-email lead nurture after the show: use genre:email_sequence_nurture (this card covers the first follow-up only)
A tagline-only back wall ('Innovating tomorrow'): visitors cannot tell what you sell; say it plainly
