cards.value_why: AWAI lists Trade Show Materials as its own project type, but in India it is usually written in-house or by the stand-design agency as part of a booth package.
cards.goal: A passer-by stops, a qualified visitor talks to staff and leaves contact details, and the follow-up earns a meeting.

structure.does: Who you serve and the outcome, with logo and one verified proof point (customer count, certification).
Three to five benefit lines, one per panel, each with one visual; placed above table height.
What it is, what it does, one number.
Two or three questions that qualify a visitor, plus one line per buyer type.
Problem, solution, proof, offer, contact and QR code; carries the detail the panels leave out.
Sent the next working day; names the expo, recalls the conversation, offers one next step.

length.note: For the whole kit. Panels are measured in words read at a distance; the handout and email carry the detail.

checklist: Does the back-wall line say who it is for and what it does in 8 words or fewer?
Can each panel line be read in about three seconds?
Are claims (customer counts, certifications, 'No. 1') verified with the client?
Is there one clear next step with a QR code or lead capture?
Does the staff script open with a question rather than a pitch?
Does the handout carry the specifications and detail the panels leave out?
Does the lead form tell visitors what their details will be used for?
Does the follow-up email name the expo and the conversation?
Are product names and terms identical across panels, handout and email?
pitfalls: Paragraphs on panels: nobody reads them while walking. Move them to the handout.
Feature lists on the back wall ('ISO 9001 | CNC | 5-axis | Pan-India'): lead with the buyer and the outcome; put specs on the labels.
Key text at the bottom of a standee: tables and visitors hide it; keep important lines at eye level.
A generic 'Thank you for visiting our stall' email: refer to what the visitor asked about and propose one specific next step.
Badge scans with no consent wording: tell visitors why you are taking their details and that they can opt out of follow-ups.
Unverified superlatives on a booth: ASCI and CCPA apply to exhibition material too; use the verified proof point instead.
cards.exemplar_brief: Booth copy kit for a Rajkot CNC machine-spares maker (fictional, 'Saurashtra Spindles'; supplied facts: spares supplied to 1,200 plants, ISO 9001 certified, 48-hour dispatch on stocked parts) at an engineering expo in Bengaluru: back-wall headline, 4 standee lines, 2 product labels, a 30-second staff opener with 3 qualifying questions, a one-page handout under 250 words and a next-day follow-up email under 120 words; English; goal: meetings with maintenance heads of auto-component plants.

verified.note: P2 S1 Sp2 V2 C1. Back-wall line says who and outcome in 7 words; dispatch kept as dispatch (no delivery claim) and tied to stocked parts everywhere; staff opener has 3 qualifying questions and per-buyer lines; handout carries detail, consent wording and a clear next step (send five part numbers); email names the expo and the conversation. Writer faults: standees 1-3 repeat the back-wall proof strip word for word and carry no visual direction (the card asks for benefit lines with one visual per panel); the follow-up says 'yesterday', which is wrong when the next working day falls after a weekend.

cards.name: Transactional email copy
cards.summary: System-triggered emails the customer expects (order confirmations, receipts, password resets, shipping and payment updates, plan changes) written so the reader understands what happened and what, if anything, to do in seconds. Good looks like a subject line that names the event and a reference, key facts at the top, one action, a light brand voice, and any promotion kept small and below the transactional content.
use_for: E-commerce order lifecycle: confirmed, shipped, out for delivery, delivered, refund processed
SaaS account emails: verify email, reset password, invoice, plan change, failed payment
Fintech and banking alerts
Travel and event bookings
Subscription renewals and expiry notices
avoid: Newsletters and offers: use genre:promotional_email
Teaching new users the product: use genre:saas_onboarding_email or genre:welcome_email_series
Cross-sell after purchase: use genre:post_purchase_email
Abandoned-cart reminders: use genre:abandoned_cart_email (commercial, needs consent rules)
Loading a transactional email with promotion: under CAN-SPAM the primary purpose decides, and a subject line read as an ad, or transactional content not mainly at the beginning, makes it commercial

cards.goal: The customer understands what happened and completes the one action, or knows no action is needed, without contacting support.

structure.does: The event plus an identifier: order number, amount or date ('Order RZ-20931 shipped: arriving 9-11 Oct').
The next most useful fact (delivery date, amount, expiry time).
What happened, in plain words.
A scannable block: items, amount, payment method (last four digits only), date, address, reference.
One button with a verb label ('Track your order', 'Reset password') and any expiry or security note.
Support route, return or exchange window, and for security emails 'Didn't request this? Do X'.
Legal entity, address, why the reader got this email; any small promotion sits below everything above.

length.note: Body words, excluding the details table and footer. Security and payment-failure emails run shortest; order confirmations carry the most detail.

checklist: Does the subject line name the event and include an identifier (order number, amount or date)?
Does the first line say what happened in plain words?
Are key details (amount, date, items, address, reference) in a scannable block near the top?
Is there one primary button whose label describes the action?
For security emails: does it say what to do if the reader did not request it, and never ask for a password or OTP by reply?
Is any promotion secondary, short and below the transactional content?
Are amounts and dates in the reader's local format (Rs 1,24,500; 9 Oct 2026)?
Is the sender name recognisable as the brand?
Is a support route stated?
pitfalls: A promotional subject line on an order email ('Your order + 20% off your next one'): it can turn the email commercial under CAN-SPAM and buries the fact the reader wanted. Put the order in the subject and the offer, if any, at the bottom.
Internal system status words ('RTO initiated', 'NDR raised'): translate to what it means for the customer and what they should do.
Vague subjects ('Your order has been updated'): say what changed.
A 'noreply' sender with no way to get help: add a support link or WhatsApp number.
Security emails that look like phishing (urgent 'verify your account' links with no context): say why the email was sent and how to check it is genuine.
Ambiguous dates and times ('delivery by 10/11'): write '10 Nov' and include the time zone for times.

cards.exemplar_brief: Order-shipped email for a Jaipur block-print apparel D2C brand (fictional, 'Rangreza'): order RZ-20931, 2 kurtas, Rs 3,480 paid by UPI, shipped with tracking link, expected delivery 9-11 Oct, 7-day exchange window; subject line, preheader and body in English with a light Hindi greeting; body under 150 words; one 'Track your order' button; a one-line fabric-care tip may follow the details; no discount promotion.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Subject names event, order number and dates; preheader adds the next fact; plain first line; scannable block (order, items, Rs 3,480 by UPI, 9-11 Oct 2026, which is Fri-Sun); one 'Track your order' button; exchange window and support route; one-line care tip after the details; footer says why the email arrived; no promotion. Only gap: the sender name is not specified.

Hotel, homestay and tour-operator blogs

Hindi and Hinglish travel blogs for domestic travellers

Ranked lists of places or hotels: use genre:best_of_roundup
Video formats: use genre:vlog_outline or genre:short_form_video_script
Writing about places you have not visited as if you had: say what you researched and what you saw, or get a contributor who went
Visa, permit and entry rules from memory: link the official source and date it

Are sponsored stays and affiliate links disclosed before the first link?
Are permit, visa and entry rules linked to the official source?
Is there an at-a-glance box near the top?
pitfalls: Brochure language ('nestled', 'hidden gem', 'breathtaking'): replace with what you saw, e.g. 'the ghat is quiet before 7 am; by 9 the boat touts arrive'.
Impossible itineraries (five sights across 80 km in one day): map the route and add travel time between every stop.
Stale prices: put a 'last checked' date on the post and on the cost table, and review before peak season.
Undisclosed free stays: ASCI's influencer guidelines and the FTC require the connection to be disclosed, close to the recommendation.
Permit rules from memory (Inner Line Permits, park entry slots): link the official page; rules change.
Rewriting other blogs' itineraries: adds nothing a search summary cannot; add your own trip notes, photos and costs.

Sunset: Ambrai Ghat is crowded from 4:45 to 5:45 pm (sunset about 5:35 pm), so arrive by 4:15 pm for a step. Museum: Mewar Textile Museum (fictional), Rs 150 entry, closed on Mondays, so schedule it for Sunday. Lake boat: 45-minute Lake Pichola ride, Rs 400 per person; the 4:30 pm slot gave the best light.

Last-checked line, at-a-glance box, disclosure before the affiliate link, pacing logic (light Day 1 after the train, museum moved to Sunday because of the Monday closure), honest crowd note on the sunset point, three stays with area trade-offs, cost table, tips. cards.name: Troubleshooting guide
cards.summary: A symptom-to-fix guide that lets a user or support agent diagnose and resolve a known problem without escalating. Good looks like a title in the user's words or the exact error text, the most common cause first, numbered single-action steps that each say how to confirm they worked, warnings before risky steps, and a clear escalation path listing what to send.
use_for: Help-centre and knowledge-base articles
Troubleshooting sections of product manuals
Support-agent playbooks and macros
Device and hardware setup issues (printers, routers, POS terminals)
Error-code references for software
avoid: Explaining how a feature works: use genre:knowledge_base_article or genre:user_manual
The error text shown in the product UI: use genre:error_messages
Short pre-sales or policy questions: use genre:faq_page
Organising by internal component or cause: users search by what they see, so organise by symptom

cards.goal: The reader resolves the problem themselves, or the support agent resolves it on the first contact.

structure.does: The symptom as users describe it, or the exact error code and text ('Error E-102: Printer not detected').
Product, version, device or OS, and anything needed before starting.
The most common cause and its fix.
In order of likelihood (or ease when equally likely): the cause in one line, numbered single-action steps with the expected result, then 'Check it worked'.
How to escalate and exactly what to include: logs, screenshots, serial or order number, what was already tried.
Links to neighbouring symptoms.

length.note: Per issue. One article per symptom keeps search and support links precise; long multi-cause issues run to the top of the range.

checklist: Does the title use the exact error text or the symptom as users describe it?
Does it say which product, version, device or OS it applies to?
Is the most common cause covered first?
Is every step a single action, numbered, starting with a verb?
Does each fix say how to confirm it worked?
Are UI labels written exactly as they appear on screen?
Are risky steps (factory reset, data loss, re-install) warned about before the step?
Is there an escalation path listing what information to send?
Can a non-expert follow it without knowing internal jargon?
pitfalls: Steps that bundle several actions ('Open Settings, go to Bluetooth and re-pair the printer'): split them so the reader can tell which one failed.
No way to tell if a fix worked: add the expected result after each fix ('The printer icon turns green').
The warning after the destructive step: put 'This deletes saved bills' before the factory-reset step.
Screenshots doing all the work: describe each step in text too, and give images alt text, so screen-reader users and search can follow.
UI labels that no longer match the app after a release: note the app version and review the article with every UI change.
'Contact your administrator' as the only escalation: say who that is, how to reach them and what to send.
cards.exemplar_brief: Help-centre troubleshooting article for a Noida POS-billing app (fictional, 'DukaanBill') on 'Bluetooth thermal printer not printing bills' on Android; audience: kirana and restaurant owners with little technical background, and the support agents who send them the link; English with the Hindi UI labels the app shows; 400-700 words; most common cause first (printer paired to another phone, or Bluetooth permission off), numbered steps with 'Check it worked' lines, a warning before the reset step, and an escalation section listing what to send support.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Symptom title, applies-to line, most common cause first (printer held by another phone) then permission (Nearby devices on Android 12+, Location on 11 and older, both correct), each fix with 'Check it worked', warning placed before the reset step and saying bills are safe, an escalation list of exactly what to send, related links. Hindi UI labels given alongside English as the brief asked (they are guesses to match to the build). Nits against the card's own pitfall: some steps bundle actions ('Open Settings, then Apps, then DukaanBill'; 'switch off, wait, switch on').

cards.name: TV / OTT / CTV commercial script (TVC)
cards.summary: A shot-by-shot script for a broadcast, streaming or connected-TV spot in two columns (video | audio), timed to the exact duration booked. OTT and connected-TV spots
Cinema advertising
Regional-language versions of a national campaign
Cutdowns from a master spot
avoid: Social-first vertical ads: use genre:video_ad_script or genre:ugc_ad_script
Audio-only spots: use genre:radio_spot_script
Long brand films and product explainers: use genre:explainer_video_script
Ads with religious or political objects, or claims of miraculous properties: barred on Indian TV by Cable Television Networks Rules rule 7

cards.goal: Viewers remember the brand and its one message, and the client and director can shoot the spot from the page.

structure.does: Client, product, title, duration, version, language(s), date.
The single idea in one sentence, for approvals.
A visual that holds a channel-surfer or a viewer about to skip; product or brand world from the start.
Story or demonstration building to the product truth; each row in two columns with a running timecode: VIDEO (one line per shot, supers) and AUDIO (VO, dialogue, SFX, music cues).
Product, logo and tagline on screen with the brand name in the VO.
Exact text, on-screen duration, same language and font as the claim, in sync with the VO.
A shorter version built from the same shoot, keeping the idea and the brand close.

length.note: The booked duration decides. Time the VO by reading aloud with a stopwatch and leave room for music, SFX and silence; a spot packed with words loses the visual idea.

checklist: Does the header state the exact duration, and do the timecodes add up to it?
Is it in two columns (video | audio) with every row timed?
Can the single idea be stated in one sentence?
Does the brand or product appear before the final shot and again at the close with logo and packshot?
Does the spot carry its message with sound off (supers) and with sound on?
Can the VO be read naturally within the timing, with room for music and SFX?
Is every factual or comparative claim substantiated, with disclaimers in the same language as the claim and in sync with the VO?
Is it free of religious or political objects and of miraculous or super-natural product claims?
Is there a cutdown version?
pitfalls: Too many words for the duration: cut VO until the read-aloud time leaves at least a second or two of air; let the picture tell part of the story.
The brand only in the last two seconds: viewers remember the story and credit a competitor. Put the product in the story.
Novel-length shot descriptions: one line per shot; the director builds the rest.
Small English disclaimers under a Hindi claim: CCPA requires the disclaimer in the same language and font as the claim, in sync with the voice-over.
An idea that lives in English wordplay: it breaks when dubbed; write ideas that transcreate, or plan language versions from the start.
Miracle claims ('hair grows back in 7 days'): barred by Cable TV rule 7(5) and, for food and oils, FSSAI's claims regulations; claim only what the client can prove.
Naming or mocking a competitor's product: comparative ads must not denigrate (ASCI Chapter IV) and can infringe the rival's trade mark.
cards.exemplar_brief: 30-second TVC script plus a 15-second cutdown for a Kochi coconut-oil brand (fictional, 'Kera Gold', cold-pressed, FSSAI-licensed) launching on Hindi general-entertainment channels and connected TV in North India; idea: a Delhi grandmother's Sunday hair-oiling ritual passed to her hostel-bound granddaughter; Hindi VO and dialogue in Devanagari with English shot descriptions; two-column VIDEO | AUDIO with timecodes; supers in Hindi; no hair-growth or medicinal claims.

verified.note: P2 S2 Sp2 V2 C1. Header, one-line idea, two-column VIDEO | AUDIO with timecodes that add to 30 s and 15 s, product in frame from 0:00 and at the close with logo, tagline and brand VO, Hindi supers that carry the story sound-off ('tel wahi, haath door'), natural Devanagari dialogue with correct gender agreement ('abhi lagati hoon'), FSSAI licence super, no claims, cutdown keeps the idea and the close. Dialogue rows at 0:03-0:08 and 0:08-0:14 are tight to read in time. Note (not a fault): the piece sits exactly at lint.max_words 400 including header and notes, so a master + cutdown kit has no headroom.
